title: Support and Resistance
short_text: Support and resistance are areas where price has previously attracted enough buyers or sellers to slow a move.
simple_explanation: Think of support as a floor and resistance as a ceiling. Price can move through either one, but traders watch these areas because many decisions tend to happen there.
example: If BTC repeatedly bounces near $60,000, that area may act as support. A trader may wait for confirmation instead of buying just because price touched the level.

title: Candlestick Psychology
short_text: A candle is not just a shape; it shows how buyers and sellers negotiated during one time period.
simple_explanation: The body shows where price opened and closed. The wicks show where price tried to go but could not hold. Long wicks often reveal rejection.
example: A long lower wick after a selloff can show sellers pushed price down, but buyers stepped in before the candle closed.

title: Trendlines
short_text: A trendline connects meaningful swing points to help visualize the current direction and rhythm of price.
simple_explanation: A trendline is a guide, not a wall. It helps you see whether price is still respecting a direction or starting to change character.
example: In an uptrend, connecting higher lows can reveal a rising support guide. A break below it may be a reason to reassess, not an automatic short signal.

title: Liquidity
short_text: Liquidity often sits near obvious highs, lows, and stop areas where many traders place orders.
simple_explanation: Markets need orders to move. Areas with clustered stops or pending orders can attract price because larger participants may find enough volume there.
example: If many traders short below a visible range low, price may dip under that low, trigger stops, and then reverse back into the range.

title: Risk Management
short_text: Risk management decides how much you can lose before the market proves your idea wrong.
simple_explanation: A good setup can still fail. Risk management keeps one failed idea from damaging the account or your decision-making.
example: If an account is $5,000 and risk per trade is 1%, the planned loss is $50. Position size should be built around that limit.

title: Stop Loss
short_text: A stop loss is a planned exit that defines where a trade idea is no longer valid.
simple_explanation: A stop is not a punishment. It is the line that says, 'My reason for entering is no longer true.'
example: If you buy after a higher low forms, a stop might sit below that higher low because a break there can weaken the setup.

title: Market Structure
short_text: Market structure describes the sequence of highs and lows that reveals trend, range, or transition.
simple_explanation: Higher highs and higher lows suggest an uptrend. Lower highs and lower lows suggest a downtrend. Mixed swings often point to a range.
example: If ETH stops making higher highs and then breaks a prior higher low, traders may treat it as a possible structure shift.

title: Breakout vs Fakeout
short_text: A breakout becomes more useful when price holds beyond a level; a fakeout fails and returns back inside the prior area.
simple_explanation: Price crossing a line is not enough. Traders often look for acceptance, volume, or a retest to reduce the chance of chasing a false move.
example: If price breaks above resistance but quickly closes back below it, the move may be a fakeout rather than a clean breakout.

title: Trading Psychology
short_text: Trading psychology is the ability to follow a plan when fear, greed, boredom, or revenge urges appear.
simple_explanation: The market can pressure you into impulsive decisions. A written plan reduces the need to decide while emotions are loud.
example: After two losses, a trader may want to double size to recover quickly. A plan can prevent revenge trading and protect the account.

title: Position Sizing
short_text: Position sizing turns a trade idea into a controlled amount of exposure based on account size, stop distance, and risk limit.
simple_explanation: The wider the stop, the smaller the position usually needs to be if your risk amount stays fixed.
example: If you risk $100 and the stop is $2 away from entry, the position is 50 units before fees and slippage are considered.
